clue.text: Electrically activated layer?

parts.note: a layer is a laying hen, and one kept in a cell-like cage reads jokingly as if it ran on electrical power cells

explanation.surface: Some device switched on by electricity that lays down a coating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Layer' suggests a coating or stratum, but here it is a bird that lays eggs; the 'electrical' part is a pun on the cages, which are stacked in rows like cells.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen kept in a small cage among many in an intensive farm is named after the rows of cells in an electrical pack.

clue.text: Not a leading character in the parable of the plough

indicators.note: the leading character of the word parable is dropped, as the clue says not to keep it

explanation.surface: A remark about a minor figure in one of the Gospel parables concerning ploughing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not a leading character' pretends to be about a minor role in a story, but means the opening letter P of 'parable' is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Land suited to ploughing and growing crops is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Sadie played in the rain

parts.note: the reading is not a girl playing outdoors in wet weather but a character Sadie who appears in the story and film titled Rain

explanation.surface: A girl called Sadie was out playing in a shower.
explanation.walkthrough: Sadie Thompson is the heroine of Somerset Maugham's story 'Rain', filmed several times; read 'the rain' as that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Maugham's South Seas tale gives its prostitute heroine Sadie this surname, and she was played on screen by Gloria Swanson and Rita Hayworth.

clue.text: It had to be carried out in case of gas attack

definitions.text: It had to be carried out in case of gas attack

parts.words: It had to be carried out in case of gas attack
parts.note: carried out sounds like a plan being executed, but means physically carried by soldiers, ready for use against poison gas

explanation.surface: A military procedure that had to be followed if poison gas was used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carried out' suggests a drill or order being executed; in fact it is an item soldiers carried with them.
explanation.definitionFit: A breathing mask that filters out poison was standard kit soldiers carried in the trenches.

clue.text: Such a plucky player, David

explanation.surface: Praise for a brave performer named David.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plucky' looks like courage, but means plucking strings; the biblical David played the harp for King Saul.
explanation.definitionFit: A musician who plucks a stringed instrument; the young David soothed Saul by playing one.

clue.text: An ointment? Right — and wrong

indicators.note: wrong signals that the letters before it are put into a mistaken, rearranged order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a salve is correct, and is told it is both correct and incorrect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' and 'wrong' look like a pair of opposite verdicts; 'wrong' mixes R plus AND into NARD.
explanation.definitionFit: Spikenard is an aromatic balm made from a Himalayan plant, mentioned in the Bible.

clue.text: Censor's final words required its deletion

definitions.text: Censor's final words required its deletion

parts.words: Censor's final words required its deletion
parts.note: the censor is Cato the Censor of Rome, who ended every speech demanding that a rival city be destroyed

explanation.surface: A censor ended by insisting that something be cut out of a text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Censor' suggests someone cutting a film or book; it is the Roman statesman Cato the Censor, who ended speeches with 'Carthago delenda est'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cato insisted the North African city, Rome's great rival, must be destroyed, and Rome razed it in 146 BC.

clue.text: Deceptive bargain may trap writer going to New York

parts.note: to trap is to catch
a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A dodgy deal could ensnare an author heading off to America.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap goods made to look attractive so as to sell quickly are described with this term.

clue.text: A student rejecting a team award, the beast

parts.note: L is a learner, the letter on a learner driver's plate

indicators.note: rejecting means the words a team award are sent back, read from the end

parts.note: a cap is awarded for selection to a national team

explanation.surface: A student turns down a sports honour, and is called a brute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejecting' turns A plus CAP into PACA; L for learner, from the British learner-driver plate, gives the student.
explanation.definitionFit: A domesticated South American animal, related to the llama, kept for its wool.

clue.text: Motorist takes Inner Circle — he's on a binge

indicators.note: takes means the motorist holds the circle within him

parts.note: a motorist is a car user
O is shaped like a circle, and inner says it goes inside

explanation.surface: A driver joins an exclusive group and then goes on a spree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inner Circle' looks like an elite group; 'takes' and 'Inner' put the round letter inside the motorist.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who drinks and makes merry noisily is a reveller at a drinking party.

clue.text: Painted new cathedral entry with excessive attention to detail

indicators.note: new signals that the letters of painted are made into a fresh arrangement
the entry, or opening, of cathedral is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone repainted the doorway of a cathedral with fussy care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges PAINTED into PEDANTI; C is the entry (first letter) of 'cathedral'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fussy person who insists on petty points of correctness is described this way.

clue.text: Information collected from all quarters

parts.note: the four quarters of the compass are north, east, west and south; this one is north
the second compass quarter here is east
the third compass quarter here is west
the fourth compass quarter here is south

explanation.surface: Information gathered from everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass points abbreviate to single letters; a popular folk etymology claims the word was formed this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Reports of recent events are what this word means.

clue.text: Relay bed-covering?

parts.note: a relay is a team of workers taking turns, and a shift is also a loose dress, so one worn in bed works as a covering

explanation.surface: A request to cover a bed again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relay' suggests laying again; it is a gang of workers who take over, and a shift is also a chemise.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers on duty through the dark hours form a team, and a shift worn to bed is a nightgown.

clue.text: Programme of up-and-coming politician is without Russian approval

indicators.note: is without means the politician has the Russian word outside it, standing in front

parts.note: someone up-and-coming is rising
da is Russian for yes
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A rising politician's policy agenda lacks the Kremlin's blessing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Programme' looks like a political manifesto; it is a TV show: Rising Damp was a 1970s British sitcom about a seedy landlord.
explanation.definitionFit: The British television sitcom starring Leonard Rossiter as a landlord ran on ITV in the 1970s.

clue.text: Unecclesiastical expressions used occasionally

parts.note: unecclesiastical splits as non-C of E, not Church of England, and the terms meant are coined for one occasion only

explanation.surface: Secular language that is used now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: CE is the Church of England, so NON-CE plays on 'unecclesiastical'; the real sense is a term coined for a single occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: Words invented for one particular occasion are given this name by lexicographers.

clue.text: Strange assortment of stones

indicators.note: an assortment is a mixture, so the letters of strange are mixed up

explanation.surface: An odd collection of pebbles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' looks like an adjective for the collection, but it is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep red semi-precious gems are a common type of these.

clue.text: Hedge to provide extra cover

explanation.surface: A bush planted to give more shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hedge' looks like a noun (a row of bushes); it is the verb, to protect against loss.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurer offsets its risk by passing some of it to another company, which also adds protection.

clue.text: Pawnee has a name for being filthy

parts.note: uncle is old British slang for a pawnbroker, the one to whom goods are pawned

explanation.surface: A Native American is known for being dirty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pawnee' looks like the Native American people; it is the person goods are pawned with, called 'uncle' in old British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dirty or impure, physically or morally, is described this way.

clue.text: Light upon unusual tree in Dyfed

indicators.note: upon in a down clue means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: a lamp gives light

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters of tree are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: A lamp shines on a strange tree in a Welsh region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges the tree into ETER, and 'upon' puts the light above it. Dyfed was a county in west Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The small university town in west Wales lies within the former county.

clue.text: This bell so funereal, so very old-fashioned

explanation.surface: A remark that a mournful church bell is quaintly dated.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is the bell tolled at a death; the second is the archaic adverb meaning 'exceedingly', as in 'passing strange'.
explanation.definitionFit: A knell rung for someone dying is named for their departure, and the old adverb meant exceedingly.

clue.text: This suit isn't ready to wear

definitions.text: This suit isn't ready to wear

parts.words: This suit isn't ready to wear
parts.note: not ready to wear sounds unfinished, but means not bought off the peg, being made to measure by a craftsman

explanation.surface: A complaint that a suit is not finished yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Isn't ready to wear' seems to mean unfinished; it means it is not off-the-peg clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing cut and sewn to an individual's measurements is the opposite of off-the-peg.

clue.text: Perverse nursery-gardener, she?

parts.note: the nursery is a nursery rhyme, whose contrary heroine is asked how her garden grows

explanation.surface: A woman who runs a plant nursery and behaves contrarily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nursery' suggests a plant nursery; it is the rhyme 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary, how does your garden grow?'.
explanation.definitionFit: The contrary girl of the rhyme grows silver bells and cockle shells in her garden.

clue.text: Something to amuse baby, or 25?

explanation.surface: A question about a toy for an infant.
explanation.walkthrough: '25' refers to the answer of 25 across, IRRITATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A noisy toy shaken by infants; as a verb it means to unsettle or fluster someone.

clue.text: About time armies kept pledges

indicators.note: kept means the armies hold the period of time within them

parts.note: a host is an army, so armies are hosts
an age is an indefinite stretch of time, roughly some time

explanation.surface: Troops finally held on to their promises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About time' looks like an exclamation of impatience; it is a long period, which 'kept' places within the armies.
explanation.definitionFit: People held as security for an agreement are human guarantees.

clue.text: Barbarous fellow became leader of hundreds

parts.note: got can mean became, as in got angry

indicators.note: the leader of hundreds is its first letter

explanation.surface: A savage man rose to command a hundred soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Goths were Germanic tribes who sacked Rome, hence a byword for an uncivilised person.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Germanic tribes that invaded Rome, hence any uncultured brute.

clue.text: To provoke angry division is about right, it appears

indicators.note: the angry word is divided and goes about the other letters, holding them within

parts.note: irate means angry
taken as written

explanation.surface: Stirring up a furious split seems to be a matter of being correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'division is about' means the angry word is split open and wraps round the abbreviation for right and 'it'.
explanation.definitionFit: To annoy or vex someone is to rouse them to anger.

clue.text: Withal, say, to anticipate what's new in Hampshire

definitions.text: to anticipate what's new in Hampshire

indicators.note: say means the phrase is spoken, the sound matching a different spelling

parts.note: withal is an old word meaning besides, for the rest

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned remark about looking forward to the latest in a southern English county.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the word that 'new' comes before in Hampshire: the New Forest, a national park there.
explanation.definitionFit: Hampshire's ancient woodland and national park is named the New one, so 'New' anticipates this word.

clue.text: Drunk, by the way, in the shopping centre

parts.note: high can mean drunk or intoxicated
a street is a way or road

explanation.surface: Someone tipsy, apparently, in the town's main shops.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the main street of a town, lined with shops, is the High Street.
explanation.definitionFit: The main road of a British town is where most of its shops are found.
